o: For each quadruple (a, b, c, m) we must test ((a^b mod 10)^c) mod m == target and collect matching indices. Example 1: index 0 gives (2^3 mod 10)^3 mod 10 = 8^3 mod 10 = 2, matching target 2; index 1 reduces mod 1 to 0; index 2 gives 6^1 mod 4 = 2 — so indices 0 and 2 are returned. Values are tiny (everything ≤ 1000), so even naive big-integer exponentiation would work in Python, but modular fast exponentiation is the clean general technique. Note the intermediate modulus is fixed at 10, so a^b mod 10 depends only on a mod 10.
k: Modular exponentiation keeps intermediates below the modulus squared, avoiding overflow.
(a^b) mod 10 only depends on a mod 10, so the first stage is cheap regardless of b.
Anything mod 1 is 0, which explains why index 1 in example 1 can never match a positive target.

a.i: Languages like Python provide three-argument pow that computes base^exp mod m efficiently via binary exponentiation. Compose two calls matching the formula exactly.
s: Keep index i if y == target.
a.t: O(q · log(max exponent)) — one binary exponentiation per stage per query, q ≤ 100
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output

a.n: Approach 2: Direct simulation with running product
a.i: Since b, c ≤ 1000 and bases after reduction are below 10, we can simulate exponentiation as a simple loop multiplying and reducing mod the target modulus each step; intermediates stay under 10·10 = 100, safe in every language.
s: Reduce a mod 10, multiply into a result b times, reducing mod 10 each step.
Then raise that result to the c-th power with running multiplication mod m.
Compare with target and record the index.
a.t: O(q · (b + c)) — linear loops over the exponents, at most ~2000 multiplications per query

w: Either approach passes easily given q ≤ 100; prefer built-in pow where available and fall back to fast exponentiation elsewhere. Pitfall: applying the modulus 10 to the wrong stage, or forgetting 1 % m for m = 1. Follow-ups: huge exponents (use Fermat/Euler reduction), or streaming queries (precompute a^b mod 10 table keyed by a mod 10).
